item.title: Trump says 'we don't need a deal with Iran' and that Vance should focus on Democrats
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Bo Erickson WASHINGTON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Thursday the US does not need a deal with Iran and directed Vice President JD Vance, who has played ‌a role in efforts to resolve the war, to focus "his complete and total attention" ‌on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states. Trump's directive came a day after the Wall Street Journal ​reported that Vance was considering face-to-face peace talks with a hard-line Iranian security official and a week after the vice president blamed the costly war with Iran for Republicans' midterm elections drubbing. Trump's comments marked a shift in tone after he had suggested in recent weeks that Iran would be ‌more willing to strike a deal ⁠in the eight-month conflict after the US elections. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds ⁠of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote on social media, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, the critical shipping route near Iran where the US military has been working to ​secure ​safe passage for international shipping. Trump said he asked Vance ​to focus instead on a domestic ‌issue the president previously put in his portfolio: leading an effort targeting alleged fraud in Democratic-run cities and states throughout the US. "Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large-scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership's blood!" Trump wrote on Thursday. Vance's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Vance ‌was considering meeting with a senior Iranian security official, ​a move that would have put Vance at the center of ​peace negotiations. Reuters has not confirmed ​the potential talks. Vance, who is viewed as a leading contender for the 2028 ‌Republican presidential nomination, distanced himself from the war ​last week after Republicans' ​midterm election rout by Democrats. The vice president blamed the costs of the Iran war in part for the party's losses. He also said an earlier recommendation to end the ​war was "sound advice." Trump responded to ‌Vance's position by defending the war as necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a ​nuclear weapon. (Reporting by Doina Chiacu, Susan Heavey, and Bo Erickson in Washington; Editing ​by Tomasz Janowski, Colleen Jenkins and Andrea Ricci ) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-says-vance-focus-domestic-133908907.html

item.title: 1 dead, 4 wounded in a shooting in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
At least five people were shot, and one was killed in Washington, D.C.’s Logan Circle neighborhood early Thursday, and police said the gunman, who was barricaded inside an apartment building, later shot himself. Officers responded to reports of an active shooting at a gym just before 8 a.m. ET, Metropolitan Police Department interim chief Jeffery Carroll said at a press briefing. Once inside, police located one victim, who died at the scene, Carroll said. Four others were transported to local hospitals, including one in critical condition. As officers were clearing the gym and an adjacent building, shots rang out from the seventh floor, where the suspect barricaded himself inside an apartment. Much of the block was cordoned off, and nearby schools were placed on temporary lockdown. While police were attempting to negotiate with the barricaded suspect, he shot himself, Carroll said. Police did not identify the gunman. Carroll said that police believe the suspect had “some sort of conflict” with the apartment building’s homeowners association. While the suspect was barricaded, a fire broke out in the building, Carroll said. The building’s sprinkler system was activated, and the fire has since been extinguished, he said. A police officer speaks to people at the scene of a shooting in Washington, D.C.'s Logan Circle neighborhood on Thursday. Aaron Schwartz/Reuters Witness Ryan Dubicki told the Associated Press that he was in his apartment around 8 a.m. when he "heard about five bangs." "They were really spread out so I thought it was construction," Dubicki said. His building's managers sent a notice about a possible active shooter. Another witness, Max Smith, told reporters that he heard gunshots and took shelter in a nearby shop. "I'm very shaken up," Smith said. "You know, you don't expect it." The shootings, which occurred just a mile from the White House, prompted a massive law enforcement response. Federal agencies, including the FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, said they sent agents to the scene to help. This is a breaking news story. Refresh this page for updates. item.title: Senators investigate whether RFK Jr. lied to Congress about his 2019 Samoa trip
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — Two Democratic senators are launching an investigation into whether Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. lied to Congress about his reason for a 2019 trip to Samoa after The Associated Press and The Guardian published documents in August refuting his testimony . The new inquiry is one of a vast array of investigations planned into the Trump administration after Democrats regained control of the House and Senate from Republicans in the midterm elections. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., said in a letter Wednesday to Children’s Health Defense, a nonprofit group known for anti-vaccine activism that was formerly chaired by Kennedy, that they were starting an investigation. The lawmakers asked the group for a broad range of documents related to Kennedy’s Samoa travel, his 2024 presidential campaign and his Senate confirmation process. The letter also requested all communications between the group and federal government officials since President Donald Trump's second term began in January 2025. The senators gave the group a deadline of Dec. 4 to comply. AP and Guardian reporting in August showed that while Kennedy repeatedly told lawmakers who held the key to his confirmation last year that his visit to Samoa before a deadly measles outbreak had “nothing to do with vaccines,” a letter he sent to the Samoan prime minister ahead of the trip on Children's Health Defense letterhead showed otherwise. In the letter, Kennedy used the words vaccine or vaccination eight times. “We intend to hold Secretary Kennedy accountable for the grave harm he has caused to vulnerable children,” Wyden and Alsobrooks wrote in their letter. “We also intend to hold him accountable for any false statements made to Congress, a crime that undermines the Senate’s ability to fulfill its constitutional duties.” The Department of Health and Human Services has maintained that the Samoa visit “was unrelated to vaccines.” In response to an AP inquiry in August, it said “any claim or insinuation based on these letters that Secretary Kennedy lied under oath or to Congress is not only false but outright defamatory.” Kennedy was not under oath during his confirmation hearing. Knowingly giving material false testimony to Congress is a crime that carries a possible prison sentence regardless of whether a person is under oath, though it is rarely prosecuted. Spokespeople for Children’s Health Defense and HHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday. Wyden is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, which has oversight into Kennedy’s health department, when Democrats retake Congress in January. Alsobrooks serves on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, which also oversees the department. The same senators on Wednesday announced a separate investigation into hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of gifts reportedly given last year to Kennedy by a donor and former employee. item.title: Planning Nvidia probes, top Democrats tell administration to 'preserve all records'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Chris Coons of Delaware have formally asked the Trump administration to "preserve all records" related to the administration's dealings with Nvidia ( NVDA ) as Democrats prepare to take power on Capitol Hill in 2027 and promise to probe the issues surrounding CEO Jensen Huang's departure. The request came in a letter Wednesday evening targeting any administration materials related to the chipmaker's exports to China, as well as the ousted CEO's affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Huang's resignation "does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren said in a statement Thursday morning adding that Trump officials must still "explain why they have not closed export control loopholes." The letter was directed to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and noted reports that Trump officials were aware of concerns about Nvidia, "yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed or other companies affiliated with the suspected operative." The White House didn't offer an immediate response Thursday morning. The letter asked the officials to confirm by next Tuesday that they will comply and have begun the document preservation process. Huang stepped down as CEO on Thursday as the scandal over his extramarital affairs quickly besieged one of the world's most valuable companies and its founder. Ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick speak in the Oval Office of the White House in July. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson A likely focus on Lutnick Warren and Coons are in line to be the heads of the Senate's powerful Banking and Foreign Relations committees and will oversee any investigations with subpoena power. Meanwhile, the still-unfolding scandal has multiple prongs that touch the White House and the Trump administration. Huang lobbied President Trump to loosen limits on advanced chips, and the White House allowed Nvidia to ship certain versions to China and other countries deemed security risks. Trump reportedly didn't take action when he learned about the possibility of a security breach and has repeatedly defended Huang in recent days, calling him "an honorable guy." Sen. Elizabeth Warren is seen on Capitol Hill this summer. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images) Andrew Harnik via Getty Images Axios reported that Trump last week ordered a crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, but that it was Lutnick who stood in the way and at least slow-walked the order's execution. That turned the focus on Lutnick, who will be under perhaps the most direct scrutiny in the months ahead. Ruben Gallego, another Democratic senator and potential 2028 presidential candidate, wrote on X that Lutnick "sold out our national security to keep the stock market high." Lutnick has also drawn scrutiny from Trump allies. "Secretary Lutnick needs to answer [why he chose to allow the sales of advanced chips] in front of God and country," Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told Politico . Steve Bannon, who served as the White House's chief strategist in the first Trump administration, recently said, "We are going to have to get to the bottom of what happened at Commerce." Letters asking for preservation of documents are a standard first step as investigations ramp up. In their letter, Warren and Coons said publicly available information "raises significant concerns about the federal government's ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security." The senators also requested a congressional briefing on possible national security risks. This story has been updated. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. This article originally appeared on Yahoo Finance at https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/planning-nvidia-investigations-top-democrats-tell-trump-administration-to-preserve-all-records-141932940.html

item.title: U.S. envoys arrive at Kremlin for Putin meeting after Ukraine talks
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Moscow after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi (Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV) Vladimir Putin indicated Thursday that Russia will not compromise on its hardline demands to end the Ukraine offensive, but offered a short-term ceasefire in a key frontline city during a Kremlin meeting with US envoys. The Russian president said he would not water down his territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine that Russia claims to have annexed, and ruled out agreeing to foreign peacekeeping troops being stationed in Ukraine -- a deployment that he said would be a "continuation of war". Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff were in Moscow after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi searching for a way to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II. Putin's comments appeared to douse hopes that a deal to end the war could be within grasp, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there was a "window of opportunity" to achieve "a result" before 2027. The Americans, meanwhile, urged Putin to allow European representatives to sit at the table for the next round of talks. Moscow has successfully managed to reframe the discussions on the war as part of a wider discussion about European security. But Kyiv and European leaders have urged against a new "Yalta" -- a reference to the post-WWII deal to carve the continent into spheres of influence -- and said talks must be focused on ending the Ukraine war first. Kushner and Witkoff will travel to Dublin, where a European summit is taking place, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky later on Thursday. - 'Continuation of war' - Usually held behind closed doors, the Kremlin chose to televise a lengthy opening exchange between Putin and the US envoys. The Russian leader rejected talk of a possible territorial settlement involving "grey" -- or demilitarised -- zones between Ukrainian and Russian positions. "For us, there is only one line of demarcation: the state border. Because then it will be clear and obvious: here are we, and here are you," he said. Russia has seized swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine since launching its full-scale offensive in 2022. That is in addition to Crimea, which it annexed in 2014, and territory that was under the control of Russian-backed separatists. Moscow has formally annexed four regions of Ukraine -- Donetsk, Kherson, Lugansk and Zaporizhzhia -- despite not having full control over them. The annexations are rejected by Kyiv and the West as illegal and not recognised by the international community. Advances by Russia's army have slowed throughout 2026 and hundreds of thousands have been killed in the almost five-year conflict, with millions more forced to flee their homes. Putin proposed organising what he called a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka, where he said some 400-500 civilians still lived. Russia claimed in the summer to have captured the city, but Ukraine insists fighting is ongoing for control. The idea would be modelled on a short-term truce that last month allowed hundreds of stranded and starving locals to flee the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. Putin also repeated his long-standing objection to any foreign troops being deployed to Ukraine as a post-war peacekeeping force -- something Kyiv says is crucial to thwarting another Russian attack. Moscow would see any foreign troops deployed in the country as a "legitimate target," Putin said, adding their deployment would be a "vicious circle" and mean "the continuation of war". - 'United vision' - European countries have been rattled by Russia pushing a review of the entire continent's security architecture, with the US also floating a new framework. That is widely seen as a reference to Moscow's long-standing demands to push back the NATO military alliance in eastern Europe and end Western military support to Kyiv. Some 50 European leaders gathered in the Irish capital Thursday, where EU chief Antonio Costa said "there is no need to reinvent the wheel" on Europe's security framework as he accused Russia of wrecking it by attacking Ukraine. French President Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Europe to rally behind a "clear and united vision" on what it wants from Ukraine talks. Russia and the United States are pushing Europe to name a single representative who they can deal with. Amid the talks, the death and destruction continued. Overnight, Russian strikes hit a residential building in Kyiv, killing one person. In Putin's home city of Saint Petersburg, a car bomb blast killed a Russian soldier -- the latest in a string of apparent assassinations of military figures inside Russia. Zelensky also reported fresh restrictions had been placed on the Starshield satellite internet service, key to Ukraine's front line communications. bur/phz This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-mediated-talks-russia-ukraine-025843578.html

item.title: Alaska judge rules Mary Peltola's request for ballot data in Senate race is 'not reasonable'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — An Alaska judge ruled Wednesday that a request by Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign for a list of absentee voters whose ballots have been rejected is “not reasonable,” particularly given the time crunch election officials face as they continue counting ballots from last week's election. Ballots are still being tallied in the ranked vote election, in which Peltola and two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan are the main contenders. Alaska’s is the only Senate race in the country that remained too early to call. The state accepts ballots up to 15 days after general elections from overseas voters, making Nov. 18 the final day to receive them. That date is also the Division of Elections’ target for conducting ranked vote tabulations if no candidate wins more than 50% of the first-choice votes. Attorneys for Peltola’s campaign last Friday sued state elections officials, seeking a list of voters whose absentee ballots have been rejected and the reasons for the rejections. They said their intent was to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. But attorneys for the state said the information requested would violate voter privacy. They also said producing such a list from a voter database would constitute an “electronic service or product” that under state law may not take priority over an agency's main responsibilities. Superior Court Judge Thomas Matthews, in a written ruling, said that “in theory” records from the voter database could be redacted and produced in a way that would allow their release. But he said the division is not required to disclose the records requested by the campaign because they “cannot reasonably be produced at this juncture, nor redacted of confidential information.” The division has deadlines to meet and says its staff is working long hours to accomplish the agency's “fundamental responsibility” of administering elections, he wrote. “The timing of the Campaign's request could simply not be worse,” Matthews wrote. An email seeking comment from one of the law firms representing Peltola's campaign was not immediately returned Wednesday, which was a holiday. The state Department of Law, which represented the Division of Elections, in a statement said it was pleased with Matthews' decision. Abha Khanna, an attorney for Peltola’s campaign, said during arguments Tuesday before Matthews the campaign wasn’t seeking to disrupt the ballot counting process. She said the absentee ballot review process was going “incredibly smoothly.” But Khanna argued the information sought is a matter of public record and in line with what campaign observers have access to in locations where absentee review boards are meeting. The campaign wanted access to that information in a more centralized way, she said. Attorneys for the state have argued that reports generated by the division with lists of ballots to be reviewed during the absentee ballot review process are not public records because they contain confidential information and are “ephemeral working documents that are not meant for preservation.” Michaela Thompson, who oversees the absentee ballot review boards for the division, said in an affidavit that the version of the report received by observers of the review process — including those affiliated with the campaigns — does not include as much confidential information but does include home addresses that many voters seek to keep private. The observers sign confidentiality agreements and cannot keep, copy or record information in the report, she said. The division’s “old, inflexible” database cannot produce a report that excludes confidential addresses, meaning the agency would have to work with a vendor to create a more tailored report, Thompson said. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/alaska-judge-rules-request-peltola-000233622.html

item.title: Hegseth honors guard who scolded him for laughter at Tomb of Unknown Soldier
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON – Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth bestowed a prestigious medal on the U.S. Army sentinel who scolded Hegseth and a group of his senior advisers for laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after a Veterans Day ceremony. Hegseth invited a group of tomb's guards, known as Army sentinels, to the Pentagon on Nov. 12, and bestowed the prestigious Joint Service Commendation Medal to the soldier who yelled at him a day earlier. We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots. https://t.co/Uk6ek6oOso — Secretary of War Pete Hegseth (@SecWar) November 12, 2026 "We love standards," Hegseth wrote in a post on social media. "Well done, Specialist." Secretary of War Pete Hegseth (L) fist bumps U.S. Secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins at the conclusion of a wreath-laying ceremony in honor of Veterans Day with U.S. President Donald Trump at The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery on November 11, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. President Trump and members of his administration visited Arlington National Cemetery to observe Veterans Day. Hegseth, his wife and a group of his senior advisers were admonished for laughing after they posed for photos in front of the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery, one of the most sacred war memorials in the country. "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times," the sentinel yelled, prompting Hegseth and other members of the group to turn around in surprise as they were walking away from the memorial. The incident was captured by television cameras and quickly went viral on social media. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is the burial site of an unidentifiable soldier who was killed in World War I. It is guarded 24 hours a day by Army sentinels, who are members of the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, an elite military unit also known as the Old Guard. Serving as a sentinel is considered to be one of the highest honors in the U.S. military. The group that posed for the photo with Hegseth included his chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver, senior adviser Tami Radabaugh and Hegseth's wife, Jennifer Hegseth. It was not clear which members of the group were laughing. The Pentagon swiftly backed the sentinel's decision to scold Hegseth and his team, writing in a statement on Nov. 11 that the "soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum." Hegseth attended the Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery with Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump , who delivered a speech at the event. During his remarks, Trump praised Hegseth for doing a "fantastic job" at the Pentagon. item.title: 'I kept the faith:' Democrat Scott Colom flips Mississippi Senate seat in historic upset
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday to flip another Senate seat for Democrats and become the first Black candidate elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi in more than 140 years. According to figures from the Associated Press, Colom — who will also be Mississippi's first Democratic senator since 1989 — won 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith finished with 48.7%. "There were times that I couldn't get donors to answer the phone," Colom told supporters as they celebrated his historic upset late Wednesday night . "They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith." Mississippi — one of the reddest states in the country — wasn't really on the national radar prior to Nov. 3. President Trump won the state by 23 percentage points in 2024 — his third straight win there. Looking ahead to the 2026 Senate race, analysts said it was a "likely Republican" hold . Barely anyone bothered to poll it . But by the end of Election Night, Colom and Hyde-Smith were separated by just 65 votes, shocking the nation. Colom's win expands Democrats' total number of Senate seats to 55 and cements the party's best overall midterm performance since 1974 — a rout that has seen the GOP lose control of the Senate, the House and statehouses across the country . As lawyers, operatives and legal observers descended on Mississippi to watch officials count every last ballot, Colom repeatedly expressed confidence that his campaign would prevail, flooding the airwaves and attending at least eight post-election events. "It's very clear the direction of this," he told reporters on Friday . Colom picked up that thread in Wednesday's victory speech. "I've been telling everybody that we're going to win this election," he said. "I was saying it 8 or 9 months ago. But every time I said it, I pointed out that people were going to give me too much credit for it because it's not something that I did. It's something that we did. All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this. I had the courage to believe in Mississippi." Hyde-Smith conceded to Colom in a video posted on X Wednesday evening : "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said. "I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state." Alaska is now the only undecided Senate race. Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan 48.9% to 47.3% with 84% of the vote counted, according to the latest AP figures. Who is Scott Colom? Colom, 43, was born in Columbus, Miss., to two lawyers who also participated in politics. In 1987, his father, Wilbur, ran for state treasurer as a Republican; his mother, Dorothy, served as the first Black Chancery Court judge in their home district. Colom earned his JD from the University of Wisconsin in 2009 and went on to serve as the first Black justice court judge in Lowndes County, Miss., before becoming the first Black city prosecutor in Columbus. In 2015, Colom defeated a nearly 30-year incumbent to become the first Black district attorney elected in a majority-white voting district in Mississippi history. He has since prosecuted a number of high-profile murder and sexual assault cases. Colom gives an update about his Senate race on Nov. 4, 2026 in Jackson, Miss. Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images In 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Colom to serve as federal judge for the Northern District of Mississippi. Leading Magnolia State Republicans — including Sen. Roger Wicker and former Govs. Phil Bryant and Haley Barbour — backed Colom's nomination. "I have known two generations of the Colom family for over 20 years and believe Scott Colom possesses the discernment to be a fair and exemplary judge," Bryant told the New York Times . But Hyde-Smith blocked Colom's nomination in the Senate, citing support his 2015 campaign received from a political action committee funded by George Soros and claiming that he favored allowing transgender athletes to compete in girls' and women's sports. The White House characterized Hyde-Smith's concerns as " spurious ." In a letter to Hyde-Smith urging her to reconsider, Colom confirmed that he had signed a letter with other prosecutors condemning efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care for transgender people, but insisted that their joint statement "did not comment on legislation specifically related to participation in athletics." Colom also said he had not known about Soros's contributions to the Mississippi Safety and Justice PAC "until I read about them in my hometown paper." Colom's unsuccessful nomination was returned to Biden on Jan. 3, 2024. In September 2025, Colom announced his U.S. Senate candidacy. How Colom won Hyde-Smith, 67, is a former lobbyist and state legislator who was serving as Mississippi's agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2018 following the resignation of Republican Sen. Thad Cochran. She won a 2018 special election and a 2020 full-term election, and she has served in the Senate ever since. There were signs before Election Day that Hyde-Smith might be vulnerable to "voter apathy," as one Mississippi State University political science professor recently put it . Sen. Wicker won reelection in 2024 by 25 points; Hyde-Smith's margin of victory in 2020 was less than half that. And while the only polls made public this cycle showed Hyde-Smith ahead , her leads were stuck in the single digits — no survey put her support above 50%. One April Democratic poll showed Hyde-Smith trailing a hypothetical "someone else" 33% to 53%. Hyde-Smith speaks at a campaign event in Corinth, Miss., on Oct. 26, 2026. Madison Thorn/Bloomberg via Getty Images Regardless, Hyde-Smith seemed content to coast to reelection, barely bothering to appear on the campaign trail. But Colom didn't have that luxury — and when he cut a viral campaign ad about beef prices in mid-October, the tide started to turn. Asked earlier this year about soaring costs, including the price of beef, Hyde-Smith told local TV station WLOX that "all commodities go through peaks and valleys," but "you have so many proteins to choose from." In the final weeks of the campaign, Colom seized on Hyde-Smith's remark about "proteins" to mock her with a spot featuring incredulous Mississippians grilling burgers, dining out and shopping for groceries — and saying they'd rather "pick another senator instead" (along with other, more colorful language). The video has since racked up nearly 19 million views on Colom's X account . She done lost her damn mind. pic.twitter.com/wHPt4PSAob — Scott Colom (@scott_colom) October 13, 2026 When the ad took off, national Democrats sprang into action. The Senate Majority PAC poured $2.2 million into the race; Senate Democrats' campaign arm contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama filmed an endorsement ad. Former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey and Raphael Warnock of Georgia rushed to Mississippi to rally with Colom. In response, Republicans were forced to play defense, sending Trump to Mississippi in the final days of the campaign (along with cash infusions of their own). In the end, it wasn't enough to get Hyde-Smith over the line. When Trump came to Mississippi, Colom attended his event to talk to rally-goers about health care, grocery bills and gas prices. "I got the best message ever for Republican voters in Mississippi," he told CNN afterward. "I'm going to get you what you were promised in 2024. You were promised lower grocery prices on Day One. That's what I will fight for. You were promised no more endless wars. That's what I will fight for. You were promised the full and transparent release of the Epstein files. That's what I will fight for." item.title: Famed ship heads for afterlife as artificial reef in deliberate sinking off Florida
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steve Gorman Nov 11 (Reuters) - Famed ocean liner SS United States, the largest passenger ship ever built in America and the world's fastest, headed for the sea floor near Florida on Wednesday in a deliberate sinking designed to transform the vessel into the world's biggest artificial reef. The finale to a ‌yearlong process preparing the ship to meet its destiny, 75 years after it was first launched at sea, was presented in a livestream with aerial views of ‌the once-grand vessel's rusted hulk, stripped of its two smokestacks, quietly, slowly settling into calm waters of the Gulf of Mexico before succumbing to the deep. The ship, measuring nearly 1,000 feet (300 m) from stem to stern, was ​surrounded by onlookers and safety crews aboard dozens of tugboats and recreational vessels that accompanied the ocean liner as it was towed out to sea for its final voyage. By then, work crews had spent months removing all environmentally unsafe materials from the ship, including residual fuel, wiring, glass, ductwork and other non-metal items, as well as any objects that could pose entanglement hazards for scuba divers. The crews then cut holes strategically throughout the ship's hull and its decks to ensure that it would sink in a gradual, level and uniform manner, according to a fact sheet ‌posted online by project organizers. No explosives were used. Passageways were ⁠also cut through the 12 decks of the interior to allow for marine life to thrive in and around the ship on the sea floor. If all goes as planned, the aging 20th-century vessel will come to rest upright on the gulf floor at a depth of 180 ⁠feet off the coast of Destin, Florida, a resort town and recreational fishing haven known for its white sand beaches and emerald green waters. The upper deck is expected to end up about 50 feet beneath the surface, organizers said. SINKING STARTS SLOWLY The sinking process began at about 1 p.m. CST but was so imperceptibly slow that the majority of the ocean liner's hull remained well above the surface ​as ​the sun set on the idle ship, surrounded by blinking lights of nearby vessels. After hours, during which ​the waterline was seen creeping up the ship's hull inches at a ‌time, the sinking accelerated as the sea poured through the holes cut into the lower decks and flooded the interior. In the final moments, livestream footage showed the ship abruptly listing to its port side before gently rolling into the sea and disappearing. Warren Jones, a spokesperson for organizers, who watched the sinking from an observation boat, said the SS United States would probably take 30 to 60 minutes to reach the seabed once the interior compartments were all completely filled with water. The SS United States, a wonder of post-World War Two oceanic luxury and engineering that carried the rich and famous across the Atlantic at speeds still unmatched, was retired from service in 1969 amid the rising popularity of commercial air travel. The ‌vessel sat moored for nearly 30 years in Philadelphia, seemingly destined to be sold for scrap, before ​authorities in Okaloosa County, in Florida's panhandle, stepped in to purchase the ship as part of a $13 million ​project. "We worked year after year to keep that ship from going to the ​scrap yard," said Jones, a boyhood passenger of the ship and representative of the SS United States Conservancy, a group that sold the ship ‌to Okaloosa County. After obtaining permission from the US Coast Guard and other ​agencies, the county had the vessel towed to ​a shipyard in Mobile, Alabama, where it was prepared for disposal at sea. The SS United States will be in good company, joining a collection of more than 500 smaller underwater sites created from the remains of various sunken ships and concrete structures to create a divers' haven known as the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Artificial Reefs. Speaking ​with Reuters by phone on Wednesday night, Jones said some wreck ‌divers were already gearing up to explore the sunken remnants of the ocean liner as early as Thursday morning. Jones, recounting vivid memories of riding the ship ​as an 8-year-old passenger with his family in 1961, said he was "comforted seeing it settle on the floor of the gulf and being embraced by ​the sea." (Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Stephen Coates and Tom Hogue) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/famed-ship-heads-afterlife-artificial-003800609.html
